\section{Introduction}

Comparing infinite processes by size fails immediately: all the processes considered here have
countably many stages, so cardinality cannot distinguish them. Comparing them by \emph{shape}
succeeds, and the invariant that does the work is the order type of the process's stages---an
ordinal.

The device that makes this concrete is a game. \textbf{Mortal} must present, in advance, a
well-ordered list of the moments of a life; the \textbf{Reaper} advances one moment per round;
Mortal survives while moments remain. The value of the game is the order type of the schedule,
and everything strategic reduces to comparison of ordinals. The model is deliberately minimal:
no strategic subtlety hides in the game tree, and every theorem is a theorem about ordinals
wearing a suggestive costume.

Two questions organise the paper. First, \emph{how much time does structural refinement buy?}
If Mortal subdivides every moment of a schedule into an infinite sequence of finer moments, how
much longer does he live? The answer---exactly a factor of $\omega$---generates a strict
hierarchy $\omega,\omega^{2},\omega^{3},\dots$; we determine where it stops and why. Second,
\emph{what is the exact reach of a bounded clock?} If a life must be timed on an odometer with
$k$ base-$\omega$ digits, what is the precise ceiling on its length, and is it attained?

We answer both, and then test the naive conjectures the answers invite. One of them---
``refinement always strictly increases the survival value''---is false, and its failure is a
diagnosis rather than an accident: it fails exactly where $\omega\cdot o=o$ has stabilised.
The last section connects the order-theoretic picture to computation, exhibiting a monotone
transfinite transition system whose closure ordinal is computed exactly and which realises the
survival game of value $\omega^{2}$ faithfully.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Notation.} Ordinals carry the usual (non-commutative) arithmetic; $\omega$ is
the first infinite ordinal. For a well-ordered set $(X,<)$, $\type(X,<)$ is its order type, and
$\rank(x)$ is the order type of the set of predecessors of $x$. For an ordinal $o$, $\Ordb(o)$
is the canonical well-ordered set of ordinals below $o$, so $\type(\Ordb(o))=o$. We write
$\Lex(A\times B)$ for the lexicographic product with the $A$-coordinate most significant, and
$\sum^{\mathrm{lex}}_{k\in\NN}X_{k}$ for the dependent sum ordered by index first. Recall
$\type(\Lex(A\times B))=\type(B)\cdot\type(A)$: the \emph{less} significant factor becomes the
left factor of the ordinal product.

\section{The model}

\begin{definition}[Survival game]
A \emph{survival game} $G$ consists of a set $\Mom(G)$ of \textbf{moments} equipped with a
well-order $<$. Its \textbf{survival value} is $\val(G):=\type(\Mom(G),<)$.
\end{definition}

The moments, in their order, are the rounds Mortal will live through; the Reaper walks the
order from the bottom; Mortal is alive while the order supplies a moment. Well-foundedness is
exactly the requirement that this walk is well defined.

\begin{definition}[Forcing]
Mortal \emph{forces survival to $\alpha$} in $G$, written $G\Vdash\alpha$, when the schedule
supplies at least $\alpha$ rounds; in the model, $G\Vdash\alpha\iff\alpha\le\val(G)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:nonforce}
If $\val(G)<\val(H)$ then $\neg\,(G\Vdash\val(H))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\val(H)\le\val(G)$ would contradict $\val(G)<\val(H)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}\label{def:basic}
The \emph{point game} $P$ has a single moment, $\val(P)=1$. The \emph{finite game} $F$ has
moments $\NN$ in their usual order, $\val(F)=\omega$: the Mortal who survives every finite
round but has no last moment. The \emph{bounded-nondeterministic game} $N$ has moments
$\Lex(\NN\times\NN)$, $\val(N)=\omega^{2}$: at each of infinitely many stages Mortal is granted
a fresh unbounded but finite reprieve.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Refinement]
For games $G,H$, the game $G\ast H$ (\emph{$G$ refined by $H$}) has moments
$\Lex(\Mom(G)\times\Mom(H))$: each moment of $G$ is replaced by an entire copy of the schedule
of $H$. The \emph{$\omega$-refinement} is $R(G):=G\ast F$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Refinement law]\label{thm:reflaw}
$\val(G\ast H)=\val(H)\cdot\val(G)$; in particular $\val(R(G))=\omega\cdot\val(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lexicographic order type of a product is the product of the order types with the
significant factor on the right: $\type(\Lex(A\times B))=\type(B)\cdot\type(A)$. Take
$A=\Mom(G)$, $B=\Mom(H)$, and specialise $H=F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Refinement never shortens a life]\label{prop:weak}
If $1\le\val(H)$ then $\val(G)\le\val(G\ast H)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$\val(G)=1\cdot\val(G)\le\val(H)\cdot\val(G)$ by weak monotonicity of multiplication in the
left factor.
\end{proof}

The weak inequality is deliberate: Theorem~\ref{thm:refute} shows the strict version is false.

\section{The finite refinement hierarchy}

\begin{definition}
$R^{0}(G):=G$ and $R^{k+1}(G):=R(R^{k}(G))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Iterated refinement law]\label{thm:iter}
For every $k\in\NN$ and every game $G$, $\val(R^{k}(G))=\omega^{k}\cdot\val(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $k$; the base case is trivial. For the step,
$\val(R^{k+1}(G))=\omega\cdot(\omega^{k}\cdot\val(G))=(\omega\cdot\omega^{k})\cdot\val(G)$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:reflaw}, the induction hypothesis and associativity, and
$\omega\cdot\omega^{k}=\omega^{1+k}=\omega^{k+1}$ since $1+k=k+1$ for finite $k$.
\end{proof}

The final step is the only use of finiteness of $k$, and it is precisely where a transfinite
version would collapse: for infinite $\delta$, $1+\delta=\delta$. This is the germ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed}.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:finval}
$\val(R^{k}(F))=\omega^{k+1}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:iter} with $\val(F)=\omega$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strictness of the hierarchy]\label{thm:strict}
If $j<k$ then $\val(R^{j}(F))<\val(R^{k}(F))$ and consequently
$\neg\,\bigl(R^{j}(F)\Vdash\val(R^{k}(F))\bigr)$: a $j$-fold refined Mortal cannot force
survival to the round at which a $k$-fold refined Mortal dies.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The values are $\omega^{j+1}$ and $\omega^{k+1}$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:finval}; exponentiation
with base $\omega>1$ is strictly increasing in the exponent and $j+1<k+1$. The forcing
statement is Lemma~\ref{lem:nonforce}.
\end{proof}

Every game in this hierarchy has countably many moments: strictness is a statement about order
structure, invisible to cardinality.

\section{Bounded-depth clocks}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{$k$-fold lexicographic natural-number clock} is $C_{k}:=R^{k}(P)$. Concretely
$\Mom(C_{k})\cong\NN^{k}$ in dictionary order with the leftmost coordinate most significant.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:ckval}
$\val(C_{k})=\omega^{k}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:iter} with $\val(P)=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The clock reads Cantor normal form]\label{prop:cnf}
The rank function of $C_{k}$ is
\[
  \rank(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})=\omega^{k-1}n_{1}+\omega^{k-2}n_{2}+\cdots+\omega\,n_{k-1}+n_{k},
\]
an order isomorphism from $\NN^{k}$ in dictionary order onto $\Ordb(\omega^{k})$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Uniqueness of the Cantor normal form of an ordinal below $\omega^{k}$ with exponents $<k$ gives
injectivity and surjectivity; monotonicity is the comparison of normal forms coefficient by
coefficient from the top, which is exactly dictionary order.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Clock characterisation]\label{thm:clock}
For any survival game $G$ and ordinal $o$,
\[
  \val(G)\le o\iff\text{there is a strictly increasing map }\Mom(G)\hookrightarrow\Ordb(o).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) An order embedding of well-orders never increases order type, so
$\val(G)\le\type(\Ordb(o))=o$. ($\Rightarrow$) If $\val(G)\le o$ then $\Mom(G)$ is
order-isomorphic to an initial segment of $\Ordb(o)$, and that isomorphism is the embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-depth clocks]\label{thm:bounded}
For every game $G$ and every $k\in\NN$, $\val(G)\le\omega^{k}$ if and only if $\Mom(G)$
order-embeds into $\Mom(C_{k})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Theorem~\ref{thm:clock} with Propositions~\ref{prop:ckval} and \ref{prop:cnf}, which
identify $\Mom(C_{k})$ with $\Ordb(\omega^{k})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $\Mom(G)$ order-embeds into $\NN$ then $\val(G)\le\omega$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$n\mapsto(\ast,n)$ embeds $\NN$ into $\Mom(C_{1})=\Lex(\{\ast\}\times\NN)$; compose and apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded} with $k=1$.
\end{proof}

The converse direction of Theorem~\ref{thm:bounded} is the assertion that the ceilings are
\emph{attained}: there is no gap between what a bounded-depth clock permits and what a Mortal
can realise on it.

\section{The limit of the finite depths}

\begin{definition}[Limit clock]
The \emph{limit clock} $L$ has moments
$\Mom(L):=\sum^{\mathrm{lex}}_{k\in\NN}\Mom(C_{k})=\{\langle k,a\rangle: a\in\Mom(C_{k})\}$,
ordered by $\langle i,a\rangle<\langle j,b\rangle$ iff $i<j$, or $i=j$ and $a<b$ in $C_{i}$.
\end{definition}

Two things must be established: that this order is a well-order at all, and that its type is
$\omega^{\omega}$. A single device does both.

\begin{definition}[Key]
$\key\langle k,a\rangle:=\omega^{k}+\rank_{C_{k}}(a)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Key bound]\label{lem:keybound}
$\key\langle k,a\rangle<\omega^{k+1}$; consequently every key is below $\omega^{\omega}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\rank_{C_{k}}(a)<\omega^{k}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:ckval}, so
$\key\langle k,a\rangle<\omega^{k}+\omega^{k}=\omega^{k}\cdot2\le\omega^{k}\cdot\omega
=\omega^{k+1}<\omega^{\omega}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Key monotonicity]\label{lem:keymono}
$\key$ is strictly increasing on $\Mom(L)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $i<j$ then
$\key\langle i,a\rangle<\omega^{i+1}\le\omega^{j}\le\omega^{j}+\rank(b)=\key\langle j,b\rangle$,
using $i+1\le j$, monotonicity of $\omega^{(-)}$, and $x\le x+y$. If $i=j$ and $a<b$ then
$\rank(a)<\rank(b)$, and adding $\omega^{i}$ on the left preserves strictness on the right
argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:wf}
The order on $\Mom(L)$ is well-founded, hence a well-order.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:keymono} it is a subrelation of the pullback along $\key$ of the well-founded
order on ordinals; pullbacks and subrelations of well-founded relations are well-founded.
Linearity and transitivity are immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The limit clock]\label{thm:limit}
$\val(L)=\omega^{\omega}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\le$) By Lemmas~\ref{lem:keybound} and \ref{lem:keymono}, $\key$ maps $\Mom(L)$ strictly
increasingly into $\Ordb(\omega^{\omega})$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:clock}. ($\ge$) For each $k$
the fibre map $a\mapsto\langle k,a\rangle$ embeds $\Mom(C_{k})$ into $\Mom(L)$, so
$\omega^{k}\le\val(L)$; since $\lambda\mapsto\omega^{\lambda}$ is normal and $\omega$ is a
limit, $\omega^{\omega}=\sup_{k}\omega^{k}\le\val(L)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:above}
$\val(R^{k}(F))=\omega^{k+1}<\omega^{\omega}=\val(L)$ for every $k$; moreover $L\Vdash\omega^{k}$
for every $k$ while $\neg\,(L\Vdash\omega^{\omega}+1)$: the limit Mortal outlives every finite
depth and dies exactly at $\omega^{\omega}$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The general mechanism}

An ordinal $o$ is \emph{additively principal} if $o>0$ and $\beta,\gamma<o\Rightarrow
\beta+\gamma<o$; these are exactly the ordinals $\omega^{a}$.

\begin{definition}[Concatenated chain]
Given games $A_{0},A_{1},\dots$, let $\Sigma A$ have moments
$\sum^{\mathrm{lex}}_{k}\Mom(A_{k})$: the lives played one after another. Put
$\Lambda_{0}:=0$, $\Lambda_{k+1}:=\Lambda_{k}+\val(A_{k})$ (the \emph{landmarks}, i.e.\ the
absolute starting times), and $\key_{\Sigma}\langle k,a\rangle:=\Lambda_{k}+\rank_{A_{k}}(a)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sigmakey}
$\key_{\Sigma}$ is strictly increasing, so $\Sigma A$ is a well-ordered game, and
$\key_{\Sigma}\langle k,a\rangle<\Lambda_{k+1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\rank_{A_{k}}(a)<\val(A_{k})$ gives the bound. If $i<j$ then
$\key_{\Sigma}\langle i,a\rangle<\Lambda_{i+1}\le\Lambda_{j}\le\key_{\Sigma}\langle j,b\rangle$
by monotonicity of the landmarks and $x\le x+y$; if $i=j$ the ranks compare strictly.
Well-foundedness follows as in Corollary~\ref{cor:wf}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:landmark}
If $o$ is additively principal, $0<o$, and $\val(A_{k})<o$ for all $k$, then $\Lambda_{k}<o$ for
all $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction: $\Lambda_{0}=0<o$, and $\Lambda_{k+1}=\Lambda_{k}+\val(A_{k})<o$ by additive
principality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Limit theorem for concatenated lives]\label{thm:sigmalimit}
Let $o$ be additively principal with $0<o$. If $\val(A_{k})<o$ for every $k$ and the values are
\emph{cofinal} in $o$ (for every $p<o$ there is $k$ with $p<\val(A_{k})$), then
$\val(\Sigma A)=o$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\le$) By Lemmas~\ref{lem:sigmakey} and \ref{lem:landmark} the key maps $\Mom(\Sigma A)$
strictly increasingly into $\Ordb(o)$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:clock}. ($\ge$) If
$\val(\Sigma A)<o$, cofinality gives $k$ with $\val(\Sigma A)<\val(A_{k})$, contradicting the
fibre embedding $\val(A_{k})\le\val(\Sigma A)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Taking $A_{k}=C_{k}$ and $o=\omega^{\omega}$ recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:limit}: the values
$\omega^{k}$ lie below $\omega^{\omega}$ and are cofinal in it by normality of
$\omega^{(-)}$ at the limit $\omega$.
\end{corollary}

Additive principality is not decoration: without it the landmarks may reach or pass $o$ and the
chain overshoots its own supremum.

\section{Structure theory}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical clock]\label{thm:canonical}
Every survival game $G$ is order-isomorphic to $\Ordb(\val(G))$ via $x\mapsto\rank(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rank map is strictly increasing, and every $\gamma<\type(\Mom(G))$ is the rank of a unique
moment.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness of the survival value]\label{thm:complete}
$\val(G)=\val(H)$ if and only if $\Mom(G)\cong\Mom(H)$ as ordered sets. Moreover every ordinal
is the value of some game.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Compose the isomorphism of Theorem~\ref{thm:canonical} for $G$ with the inverse
of the one for $H$. ($\Leftarrow$) Isomorphic well-orders have equal type. Surjectivity: take
the game with moments $\Ordb(o)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$G\frown H$ is the game with moments $\Mom(G)\sqcup_{\mathrm{lex}}\Mom(H)$: all of $G$'s
moments, in order, then all of $H$'s.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:concat}
$\val(G\frown H)=\val(G)+\val(H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Non-commutativity of lives]\label{thm:noncomm}
$\val(F\frown P)=\omega+1\neq\omega=1+\omega=\val(P\frown F)$: an extra moment appended
\emph{after} an $\omega$-life is a genuine gain, while the same moment prefixed \emph{before}
it is invisible.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:concat} together with $1+\omega=\omega$ and $\omega<\omega+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
An ordinal $o$ is \emph{refinement stable} when $\omega\cdot o=o$; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:reflaw} this says exactly that $\val(R(G))=\val(G)$ for a game of value $o$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Stability criterion in the pure scale]\label{thm:stability}
For every ordinal $a$: $\omega^{a}$ is refinement stable if and only if $\omega\le a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\omega\cdot\omega^{a}=\omega^{1+a}$, so stability says $\omega^{1+a}=\omega^{a}$, equivalent
by injectivity of $\lambda\mapsto\omega^{\lambda}$ to $1+a=a$. For finite $a=n$,
$1+n=n+1\neq n$; for $\omega\le a$, $1+a=a$ by left absorption.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Every finite depth value $\omega^{k+1}$ is unstable---refinement genuinely helps there---while
$\omega^{\omega}$ is stable.
\end{corollary}

\section{A negative result: refinement is not always a gain}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed point]\label{thm:fixed}
$\val(R(L))=\val(L)$, i.e.\ $\omega\cdot\omega^{\omega}=\omega^{\omega}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\omega\cdot\omega^{\omega}=\omega^{1+\omega}=\omega^{\omega}$ since $1+\omega=\omega$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Refutation of strict refinement]\label{thm:refute}
It is \emph{not} the case that for all games $G,H$ with $0<\val(G)$ and $1<\val(H)$ one has
$\val(G)<\val(G\ast H)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $G=L$, $H=F$: then $\val(L)=\omega^{\omega}>0$, $\val(F)=\omega>1$, and
$\val(L\ast F)=\omega\cdot\omega^{\omega}=\omega^{\omega}=\val(L)$ by
Theorems~\ref{thm:reflaw} and \ref{thm:fixed}.
\end{proof}

The formal cause is that ordinal multiplication is only weakly monotone in its left factor. The
structural cause is more illuminating: a schedule that already contains, cofinally, blocks of
every finite base-$\omega$ depth is unchanged, up to isomorphism, by one more layer of
subdivision. The factor of $\omega$ is real at every finite depth and disappears exactly at the
additively principal ordinals with infinite exponent---which is Theorem~\ref{thm:stability}.

\section{A monotone transfinite machine with closure ordinal exactly $\omega^{2}$}

Fix the bounded-nondeterministic game $N$ of Definition~\ref{def:basic}, $\val(N)=\omega^{2}$.

\begin{definition}[Cells and step]
The \emph{cells} are the moments of $N$. For a set $S$ of cells,
$\stepop(S):=\{x:\forall y<x,\ y\in S\}$: a cell switches on once all strictly earlier cells are
on. The operator $\stepop$ is monotone with respect to inclusion.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Stages]
By recursion on ordinals,
$\stg(\alpha):=\stepop\bigl(\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}\stg(\beta)\bigr)$; this single clause
packages the successor rule and the limit rule. The \emph{arrival time} of a cell is
$\arrv(x):=\rank_{N}(x)<\omega^{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form of the stages]\label{thm:closedform}
For every ordinal $\alpha$ and cell $x$: $x\in\stg(\alpha)\iff\arrv(x)\le\alpha$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, $\arrv(x)\le\alpha\iff\forall y<x,\ \arrv(y)<\alpha$: left to right is monotonicity of
rank; right to left, if $\arrv(x)>\alpha$ then $\alpha<\omega^{2}$ is the arrival time of a
unique cell $y$, and $y<x$, contradicting $\arrv(y)<\alpha$. Now induct on $\alpha$. If
$x\in\stg(\alpha)$ then every $y<x$ lies in some $\stg(\beta)$ with $\beta<\alpha$, so
$\arrv(y)\le\beta<\alpha$, whence $\arrv(x)\le\alpha$. Conversely if $\arrv(x)\le\alpha$ and
$y<x$ then $\arrv(y)<\alpha$ and the induction hypothesis puts $y\in\stg(\arrv(y))$, one of the
unioned stages; so $x\in\stg(\alpha)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit successor and limit rules]
$\stg(\alpha+1)=\stepop(\stg(\alpha))$, and at every $\alpha$ (in particular at limits)
$\stg(\alpha)=\stepop(\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}\stg(\beta))$. The stages are monotone in $\alpha$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The second is the definition; for the first, unwind both sides through
Theorem~\ref{thm:closedform}: $\arrv(x)\le\alpha+1$ iff every $y<x$ has $\arrv(y)\le\alpha$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$\alpha$ is \emph{terminal} when $\stg(\alpha+1)=\stg(\alpha)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact closure ordinal]\label{thm:closure}
$\omega^{2}$ is the least terminal time: no $\alpha<\omega^{2}$ is terminal, and $\omega^{2}$
is.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\alpha<\omega^{2}$. Since $\omega^{2}$ is additively principal and $1<\omega^{2}$, also
$\alpha+1<\omega^{2}$, so some cell $x$ has $\arrv(x)=\alpha+1$; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:closedform}, $x\in\stg(\alpha+1)\setminus\stg(\alpha)$. Conversely every cell
has arrival time below $\omega^{2}$, so $\stg(\omega^{2})=\stg(\omega^{2}+1)$ is the set of all
cells.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Faithfulness]\label{thm:faithful}
$\arrv$ is a strictly increasing bijection from the cells onto the ordinals below $\omega^{2}$;
hence the reachable-time well-order of the machine is order-isomorphic to the moments of $N$,
and the least terminal time equals $\val(N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strict monotonicity and injectivity are properties of rank; surjectivity is
Theorem~\ref{thm:canonical} applied to $N$. A strictly monotone surjection of linear orders is
an order isomorphism. Combine with Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}.
\end{proof}

Thus the machine is not merely \emph{some} system with closure ordinal $\omega^{2}$: its clock
of reachable times is literally the game's schedule, and the point at which the computation
stalls is the point at which Mortal dies.

\section{Algorithms}

All procedures operate on ordinals below $\varepsilon_{0}$ in Cantor normal form, represented as
strictly decreasing lists of (exponent, coefficient) pairs whose exponents are recursively of
the same shape.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\Alph*)]
\item \textbf{Cantor normal form arithmetic.} Comparison is lexicographic on the term list.
Addition $\alpha+\beta$ deletes from $\alpha$ every term whose exponent is strictly below the
leading exponent of $\beta$ (left absorption made concrete), merges an equal leading exponent by
adding coefficients, and appends $\beta$. Multiplication distributes over the terms of the right
factor: a finite term scales the leading coefficient of the left factor and re-appends its tail,
while a term $\omega^{e}c$ yields $\omega^{(\text{lead exponent of }\alpha)+e}c$. Each operation
is linear in the number of terms up to recursive exponent comparisons.

\item \textbf{Clock reading and its inverse.} The rank map
$(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})\mapsto\sum_{i}\omega^{k-i}n_{i}$ converts a moment into an ordinal in
$O(k)$ operations, and uniqueness of the normal form converts back; this makes the embeddings of
Theorems~\ref{thm:clock}--\ref{thm:bounded} executable on concrete data.

\item \textbf{Key evaluation and monotonicity certification.} $\key\langle k,a\rangle=
\omega^{k}+\rank(a)$ is evaluated in $O(k)$ and, by Lemmas~\ref{lem:keybound} and
\ref{lem:keymono}, certifies both well-foundedness of the dependent lexicographic order and the
bound $\val(L)\le\omega^{\omega}$; comparing two keys is a comparison of normal forms.

\item \textbf{Stage evaluation.} Theorem~\ref{thm:closedform} replaces the transfinite recursion
defining $\stg(\alpha)$ with the $O(1)$ membership test $\arrv(x)\le\alpha$; a non-terminality
witness at $\alpha$ is obtained by decoding $\alpha+1<\omega^{2}$ into the unique cell of that
arrival time.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Order type, not cardinality.} Every game here has countably many moments, so every
strict inequality proved is invisible to counting and visible only to order. The model makes
this unavoidable: forcing survival to $\alpha$ \emph{is} the inequality $\alpha\le\val(G)$, and
by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} the strategic and the ordinal hierarchies are the same object.

\textbf{One identity behind three theorems.} The finite hierarchy is strict because $1+k=k+1$
for finite $k$; the limit is stable because $1+\omega=\omega$; refinement stability of
$\omega^{a}$ is exactly $1+a=a$. Theorems~\ref{thm:iter}, \ref{thm:stability} and
\ref{thm:fixed} are three views of one fact about left absorption, which also explains why the
naive strictness conjecture fails at a computable boundary rather than sporadically.

\textbf{Keys as certificates.} A strictly monotone map into the ordinals is simultaneously a
proof of well-foundedness, an upper bound on order type, and an executable comparison
procedure. Dependent lexicographic sums are a case where the abstract fact is standard but the
usable witness is not automatic; the landmark key $\Lambda_{k}+\rank(a)$ supplies it in general.

\textbf{Additive principality as the right hypothesis.} Theorem~\ref{thm:sigmalimit} isolates
why $\omega^{\omega}$ appears: it is the least additively principal ordinal above all
$\omega^{k}$. Its two hypotheses are complementary---cofinality forces the value up to $o$,
additive principality prevents the landmarks from pushing it past $o$.

\textbf{Closure ordinals.} Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} computes a closure ordinal exactly in both
directions, which is the interesting half of such statements. The step operator is, however,
allowed to consult the whole earlier configuration; restricting to more finitely presented step
operators is the natural next question.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The transfinite refinement tower and $\varepsilon_{0}$.} Extend $R^{k}$ to a
tower indexed by ordinals, refining by $\omega$ at successors and taking the dependent
lexicographic sum at limits. Conjecturally level $\delta$ over the finite game has value
$\omega^{\delta+1}$ for every $\delta$ below the first fixed point of
$\delta\mapsto\omega^{\delta}$, and the tower's own limit is exactly $\varepsilon_{0}$. The key
insight is that the level-$k$ bound proved here comes entirely from the key
$\omega^{k}+\rank(a)$, which is definable uniformly in the level; replacing $k$ by an ordinal
turns the finite normal-form argument into the general one, so only a type-level transfinite
recursion remains, the general limit step being Theorem~\ref{thm:sigmalimit}.

\item \textbf{Refinement stability as a normal-form tail condition.} The general criterion
should read: $\omega\cdot o=o$ if and only if $o=0$ or every Cantor exponent of $o$ is
infinite. Multiplication by $\omega$ shifts each exponent $e$ to $1+e$, and $1+e=e$ is
equivalent to $\omega\le e$, so stability is a tail condition, not a size condition.

\item \textbf{A clockability gap for finitely presented steps.} Restricting the step operator to
a fixed finite amount of local data should make some ordinals unattainable as closure ordinals;
identifying the least such ordinal is the concrete target.

\item \textbf{Non-well-ordered schedules.} If Mortal may present a merely linearly ordered
schedule, replace the order type by the ordinal of the well-founded part and ask how much of the
theory survives.

\item \textbf{Quantitative forcing.} Enriching forcing with resource bounds---requiring each
moment to be named inside a fixed notation system---would connect the hierarchy to ordinal
notation systems, where $\omega^{\omega}$ and $\varepsilon_{0}$ have independent significance.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

The survival game reduces the question of outliving an adversary to a question about order
types, faithfully and without loss. Within that dictionary, structural refinement is worth
exactly one factor of $\omega$, and iterating it produces a strict hierarchy
$\omega,\omega^{2},\omega^{3},\dots$ whose members are exactly the ordinals timed by base-$\omega$
odometers of bounded digit length, with the ceilings attained. Stacking all finite depths gives
exactly $\omega^{\omega}$, by way of a key function that doubles as a well-foundedness
certificate, and this is an instance of a general limit theorem over additively principal
ordinals. At $\omega^{\omega}$ refinement becomes idempotent, refuting the natural conjecture
that refinement always strictly helps, the exact boundary being the absorption identity
$1+a=a$. Finally, a monotone transfinite transition system built on the $\omega^{2}$-clock has
closure ordinal exactly $\omega^{2}$, with its reachable-time well-order isomorphic to the game
it realises: length of life, order type, positional notation and closure ordinal are four
descriptions of one thing.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import product
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exact ordinal arithmetic below epsilon_0, in Cantor normal form.
#
# An ordinal is a strictly decreasing list of (exponent, coefficient) pairs
#     omega^e_1 * c_1 + ... + omega^e_m * c_m ,   e_1 > ... > e_m,  c_i >= 1,
# where each exponent is itself an ordinal in the same representation.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ord:
    """A countable ordinal below epsilon_0, in Cantor normal form."""

    terms: Tuple[Tuple["Ord", int], ...] = ()

    # -- constructors -------------------------------------------------------

    @staticmethod
    def zero() -> "Ord":
        return Ord(())

    @staticmethod
    def finite(n: int) -> "Ord":
        if n < 0:
            raise ValueError("ordinals are non-negative")
        return Ord(()) if n == 0 else Ord(((Ord.zero(), n),))

    @staticmethod
    def omega_pow(exponent: "Ord", coeff: int = 1) -> "Ord":
        """omega^exponent * coeff."""
        if coeff == 0:
            return Ord.zero()
        return Ord(((exponent, coeff),))

    # -- basic predicates ---------------------------------------------------

    @property
    def is_zero(self) -> bool:
        return len(self.terms) == 0

    @property
    def is_finite(self) -> bool:
        return self.is_zero or (len(self.terms) == 1 and self.terms[0][0].is_zero)

    @property
    def finite_part(self) -> int:
        if self.terms and self.terms[-1][0].is_zero:
            return self.terms[-1][1]
        return 0

    # -- comparison ---------------------------------------------------------

    def cmp(self, other: "Ord") -> int:
        """Return -1, 0, +1 according as self <, =, > other."""
        for (e1, c1), (e2, c2) in zip(self.terms, other.terms):
            k = e1.cmp(e2)
            if k != 0:
                return k
            if c1 != c2:
                return -1 if c1 < c2 else 1
        if len(self.terms) == len(other.terms):
            return 0
        return -1 if len(self.terms) < len(other.terms) else 1

    def __lt__(self, other: "Ord") -> bool:
        return self.cmp(other) < 0

    def __le__(self, other: "Ord") -> bool:
        return self.cmp(other) <= 0

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:  # type: ignore[override]
        return isinstance(other, Ord) and self.cmp(other) == 0

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash(self.terms)

    # -- arithmetic ---------------------------------------------------------

    def __add__(self, other: "Ord") -> "Ord":
        """Ordinal addition (absorbs strictly smaller leading terms on the left)."""
        if other.is_zero:
            return self
        lead = other.terms[0][0]
        kept = [(e, c) for (e, c) in self.terms if lead < e]
        merged: List[Tuple[Ord, int]] = list(kept)
        tail = list(other.terms)
        # a term of self with exponent exactly `lead` merges coefficients
        same = [c for (e, c) in self.terms if e == lead]
        if same:
            e0, c0 = tail[0]
            tail[0] = (e0, c0 + same[0])
        return Ord(tuple(merged + tail))

    def __mul__(self, other: "Ord") -> "Ord":
        """Ordinal multiplication self * other (left factor applied `other` times)."""
        if self.is_zero or other.is_zero:
            return Ord.zero()
        lead_e, lead_c = self.terms[0]
        out = Ord.zero()
        for (e, c) in other.terms:
            if e.is_zero:
                # self * c  =  omega^lead_e * (lead_c * c) + (rest of self)
                head = Ord.omega_pow(lead_e, lead_c * c)
                rest = Ord(self.terms[1:])
                out = out + head + rest
            else:
                out = out + Ord.omega_pow(lead_e + e, c)
        return out

    def omega_times(self) -> "Ord":
        """omega * self."""
        return OMEGA * self

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        if self.is_zero:
            return "0"
        pieces: List[str] = []
        for (e, c) in self.terms:
            if e.is_zero:
                pieces.append(str(c))
            else:
                if e == ONE:
                    base = "w"
                elif e.is_finite:
                    base = f"w^{e}"
                else:
                    base = f"w^({e})"
                pieces.append(base if c == 1 else f"{base}*{c}")
        return " + ".join(pieces)


ZERO = Ord.zero()
ONE = Ord.finite(1)
OMEGA = Ord.omega_pow(ONE)
OMEGA_SQ = Ord.omega_pow(Ord.finite(2))
OMEGA_OMEGA = Ord.omega_pow(OMEGA)


def omega_pow_nat(k: int) -> Ord:
    """omega^k for a natural number k."""
    return ONE if k == 0 else Ord.omega_pow(Ord.finite(k))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The refinement law and the finite hierarchy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def refine_value(v: Ord) -> Ord:
    """Survival value after one omega-refinement:  omega * v."""
    return OMEGA * v


def iterated_refinement_value(k: int, base: Ord) -> Ord:
    """Survival value of the k-fold refinement of a game of value `base`."""
    v = base
    for _ in range(k):
        v = refine_value(v)
    return v


def demo_hierarchy(max_k: int = 5) -> None:

        want = omega_pow_nat(k + 1)

    ok = all(

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Bounded-depth clocks: the k-fold lexicographic natural-number clock
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Moment = Tuple[int, ...]  # a moment of natClock(k) is a k-tuple of naturals


def clock_reading(m: Moment) -> Ord:
    """
    The order-theoretic position (the `typein`) of a moment of the k-fold
    lexicographic natural-number clock:

        (n_1, ..., n_k)  |-->  omega^(k-1) n_1 + ... + omega n_(k-1) + n_k.

    The most significant coordinate is the leftmost one.
    """
    k = len(m)
    out = ZERO
    for i, n in enumerate(m):
        if n:
            out = out + Ord.omega_pow(Ord.finite(k - 1 - i), n)
    return out


def lex_less(a: Moment, b: Moment) -> bool:
    """Lexicographic order on equal-length tuples, most significant first."""
    return a < b


def sample_moments(k: int, bound: int) -> Iterator[Moment]:
    yield from product(range(bound), repeat=k)


def demo_bounded_depth_clocks(max_k: int = 3, bound: int = 4) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. BOUNDED-DEPTH CLOCKS AND THE EMBEDDING CHARACTERISATION")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("The k-fold clock is N^k in lexicographic order; its reading map is an")
    print("order isomorphism onto the ordinals below omega^k.  A game is clocked")
    print("by it exactly when its survival value is at most omega^k.\n")
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        moments = list(sample_moments(k, bound))
        readings = [clock_reading(m) for m in moments]
        mono = all(
            (clock_reading(a) < clock_reading(b)) == lex_less(a, b)
            for a in moments
            for b in moments
            if a != b
        )
        below = all(r < omega_pow_nat(k) for r in readings)
        print(f"  k = {k}: reading map order-faithful on {len(moments)} sampled moments: {mono}")
        print(f"         every reading below omega^{k}: {below}")
    print("\n  Sample readings in the 3-fold clock:")
    for m in [(0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 7), (0, 2, 5), (1, 0, 0), (4, 3, 2)]:
        print(f"    {str(m):>12}  ->  {clock_reading(m)!r}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The limit clock and the key function
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

LimitMoment = Tuple[int, Moment]  # <k, a> with a a moment of natClock(k)


def limit_key(x: LimitMoment) -> Ord:
    """key<k, a> = omega^k + reading(a)."""
    k, a = x
    return omega_pow_nat(k) + clock_reading(a)


def limit_lex_less(x: LimitMoment, y: LimitMoment) -> bool:
    """Lexicographic order on the dependent sum: compare depth first."""
    if x[0] != y[0]:
        return x[0] < y[0]
    return lex_less(x[1], y[1])


def demo_limit_clock(max_k: int = 3, bound: int = 3) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. THE LIMIT CLOCK HAS VALUE EXACTLY omega^omega")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("Stack all finite-depth clocks lexicographically.  The key function")
    print("key<k, a> = omega^k + reading(a) is strictly increasing and lands")
    print("strictly below omega^omega, which bounds the value; the individual")
    print("depths are cofinal, which forces equality.\n")
    pts: List[LimitMoment] = []
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        for a in sample_moments(k, bound):
            pts.append((k, a))
    mono = all(
        (limit_key(x) < limit_key(y)) == limit_lex_less(x, y)
        for x in pts
        for y in pts
        if x != y
    )
    below = all(limit_key(x) < OMEGA_OMEGA for x in pts)
    print(f"  key strictly monotone on {len(pts)} sampled moments: {mono}")
    print(f"  every key strictly below omega^omega:              {below}")

    for x in [(1, (0,)), (1, (5,)), (2, (0, 0)), (2, (3, 1)), (4, (1, 0, 0, 2))]:

    for k in range(4):

    print()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The monotone transfinite machine with closure ordinal omega^2
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cell = Tuple[int, int]  # cell (m, n) has arrival time omega*m + n


def arrival(cell: Cell) -> Ord:
    m, n = cell
    return (OMEGA * Ord.finite(m)) + Ord.finite(n)


def decode_cell(alpha: Ord) -> Cell:
    """The unique cell whose arrival time is alpha, for alpha < omega^2."""
    if not alpha < OMEGA_SQ:
        raise ValueError("only cells below omega^2 exist")
    m = 0
    for (e, c) in alpha.terms:
        if e == ONE:
            m = c
    return (m, alpha.finite_part)


def stage_contains(alpha: Ord, cell: Cell) -> bool:
    """Closed form of the stages: cell is on at time alpha iff arrival <= alpha."""
    return arrival(cell) <= alpha


def step(on: Iterable[Cell], universe: Sequence[Cell]) -> List[Cell]:
    """One transition: a cell switches on once all strictly earlier cells are on."""
    on_set = set(on)
    out: List[Cell] = []
    for c in universe:
        if all(d in on_set for d in universe if arrival(d) < arrival(c)):
            out.append(c)
    return out


def demo_machine(rows: int = 3, cols: int = 6) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. A MONOTONE TRANSFINITE MACHINE WITH CLOSURE ORDINAL omega^2")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("Cells are the moments of the omega^2 clock: cell (m, n) has arrival")
    print("time omega*m + n.  A cell switches on once all strictly earlier cells")
    print("are on; at limit times the machine unions all earlier configurations.\n")
    universe = [(m, n) for m in range(rows) for n in range(cols)]
    universe.sort(key=lambda c: (c[0], c[1]))

    # verify the closed form against a direct simulation on finite initial times
    print("  Successor rule agrees with the closed form on finite times:")
    ok = True
    for t in range(cols):
        alpha = Ord.finite(t)
        closed = {c for c in universe if stage_contains(alpha, c)}
        simulated = set(step({c for c in universe if stage_contains(Ord.finite(t - 1), c)}
                             if t > 0 else set(), universe))
        # restrict the comparison to the finite window actually determined
        closed_w = {c for c in closed if c[0] == 0}
        simulated_w = {c for c in simulated if c[0] == 0}
        ok = ok and closed_w == simulated_w
    print(f"    {ok}\n")

    print("  Stages (rows = the omega-blocks m, columns = offsets n, '#' = on):")
    for label, alpha in [("t = 0", ZERO), ("t = 3", Ord.finite(3)),
                         ("t = omega", OMEGA), ("t = omega+2", OMEGA + Ord.finite(2)),
                         ("t = omega*2", OMEGA * Ord.finite(2))]:
        print(f"    {label:>12}: ", end="")
        for m in range(rows):
            row = "".join("#" if stage_contains(alpha, (m, n)) else "." for n in range(cols))
            print(f"[{row}]", end=" ")
        print()
    print()
    print("  No stage below omega^2 is terminal: for every alpha < omega^2 the")
    print("  cell with arrival time alpha+1 is off at alpha and on at alpha+1.")
    for alpha in [ZERO, Ord.finite(5), OMEGA, OMEGA * Ord.finite(3) + Ord.finite(2)]:
        succ = alpha + ONE
        witness = decode_cell(succ)
        appears = (not stage_contains(alpha, witness)) and stage_contains(succ, witness)
        print(f"    alpha = {alpha!r:>14}:  alpha+1 = {succ!r:>16} < omega^2: "
              f"{succ < OMEGA_SQ}   new cell {str(witness):>8} appears: {appears}")
    print("\n  At time omega^2 every cell is on, so the machine is terminal there;")
    print("  hence its closure ordinal is exactly omega^2, which is precisely the")
    print("  survival value of the bounded-nondeterministic game it realises.\n")

def demo_general_limit(max_k: int = 5) -> None:

        landmark = landmark + val
    print("\n  Landmarks stay below omega^omega (additive principality), and")
    print("  omega^k is cofinal in omega^omega, so the total value is omega^omega.\n")

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import product
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exact ordinal arithmetic below epsilon_0, in Cantor normal form.
#
# An ordinal is a strictly decreasing list of (exponent, coefficient) pairs
#     omega^e_1 * c_1 + ... + omega^e_m * c_m ,   e_1 > ... > e_m,  c_i >= 1,
# where each exponent is itself an ordinal in the same representation.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ord:
    """A countable ordinal below epsilon_0, in Cantor normal form."""

    terms: Tuple[Tuple["Ord", int], ...] = ()

    # -- constructors -------------------------------------------------------

    @staticmethod
    def zero() -> "Ord":
        return Ord(())

    @staticmethod
    def finite(n: int) -> "Ord":
        if n < 0:
            raise ValueError("ordinals are non-negative")
        return Ord(()) if n == 0 else Ord(((Ord.zero(), n),))

    @staticmethod
    def omega_pow(exponent: "Ord", coeff: int = 1) -> "Ord":
        """omega^exponent * coeff."""
        if coeff == 0:
            return Ord.zero()
        return Ord(((exponent, coeff),))

    # -- basic predicates ---------------------------------------------------

    @property
    def is_zero(self) -> bool:
        return len(self.terms) == 0

    @property
    def is_finite(self) -> bool:
        return self.is_zero or (len(self.terms) == 1 and self.terms[0][0].is_zero)

    @property
    def finite_part(self) -> int:
        if self.terms and self.terms[-1][0].is_zero:
            return self.terms[-1][1]
        return 0

    # -- comparison ---------------------------------------------------------

    def cmp(self, other: "Ord") -> int:
        """Return -1, 0, +1 according as self <, =, > other."""
        for (e1, c1), (e2, c2) in zip(self.terms, other.terms):
            k = e1.cmp(e2)
            if k != 0:
                return k
            if c1 != c2:
                return -1 if c1 < c2 else 1
        if len(self.terms) == len(other.terms):
            return 0
        return -1 if len(self.terms) < len(other.terms) else 1

    def __lt__(self, other: "Ord") -> bool:
        return self.cmp(other) < 0

    def __le__(self, other: "Ord") -> bool:
        return self.cmp(other) <= 0

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:  # type: ignore[override]
        return isinstance(other, Ord) and self.cmp(other) == 0

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash(self.terms)

    # -- arithmetic ---------------------------------------------------------

    def __add__(self, other: "Ord") -> "Ord":
        """Ordinal addition (absorbs strictly smaller leading terms on the left)."""
        if other.is_zero:
            return self
        lead = other.terms[0][0]
        kept = [(e, c) for (e, c) in self.terms if lead < e]
        merged: List[Tuple[Ord, int]] = list(kept)
        tail = list(other.terms)
        # a term of self with exponent exactly `lead` merges coefficients
        same = [c for (e, c) in self.terms if e == lead]
        if same:
            e0, c0 = tail[0]
            tail[0] = (e0, c0 + same[0])
        return Ord(tuple(merged + tail))

    def __mul__(self, other: "Ord") -> "Ord":
        """Ordinal multiplication self * other (left factor applied `other` times)."""
        if self.is_zero or other.is_zero:
            return Ord.zero()
        lead_e, lead_c = self.terms[0]
        out = Ord.zero()
        for (e, c) in other.terms:
            if e.is_zero:
                # self * c  =  omega^lead_e * (lead_c * c) + (rest of self)
                head = Ord.omega_pow(lead_e, lead_c * c)
                rest = Ord(self.terms[1:])
                out = out + head + rest
            else:
                out = out + Ord.omega_pow(lead_e + e, c)
        return out

    def omega_times(self) -> "Ord":
        """omega * self."""
        return OMEGA * self

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        if self.is_zero:
            return "0"
        pieces: List[str] = []
        for (e, c) in self.terms:
            if e.is_zero:
                pieces.append(str(c))
            else:
                if e == ONE:
                    base = "w"
                elif e.is_finite:
                    base = f"w^{e}"
                else:
                    base = f"w^({e})"
                pieces.append(base if c == 1 else f"{base}*{c}")
        return " + ".join(pieces)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Bounded-depth clocks: the k-fold lexicographic natural-number clock
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Moment = Tuple[int, ...]  # a moment of natClock(k) is a k-tuple of naturals


def clock_reading(m: Moment) -> Ord:
    """
    The order-theoretic position (the `typein`) of a moment of the k-fold
    lexicographic natural-number clock:

        (n_1, ..., n_k)  |-->  omega^(k-1) n_1 + ... + omega n_(k-1) + n_k.

    The most significant coordinate is the leftmost one.
    """
    k = len(m)
    out = ZERO
    for i, n in enumerate(m):
        if n:
            out = out + Ord.omega_pow(Ord.finite(k - 1 - i), n)
    return out


def lex_less(a: Moment, b: Moment) -> bool:
    """Lexicographic order on equal-length tuples, most significant first."""
    return a < b


def sample_moments(k: int, bound: int) -> Iterator[Moment]:
    yield from product(range(bound), repeat=k)


def demo_bounded_depth_clocks(max_k: int = 3, bound: int = 4) -> None:

    print("order isomorphism onto the ordinals below omega^k.  A game is clocked")
    print("by it exactly when its survival value is at most omega^k.\n")
    for k in range(1, max_k + 1):
        moments = list(sample_moments(k, bound))
        readings = [clock_reading(m) for m in moments]
        mono = all(
            (clock_reading(a) < clock_reading(b)) == lex_less(a, b)
            for a in moments
            for b in moments
            if a != b
        )
        below = all(r < omega_pow_nat(k) for r in readings)
        print(f"  k = {k}: reading map order-faithful on {len(moments)} sampled moments: {mono}")
        print(f"         every reading below omega^{k}: {below}")
    print("\n  Sample readings in the 3-fold clock:")
    for m in [(0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 7), (0, 2, 5), (1, 0, 0), (4, 3, 2)]:
        print(f"    {str(m):>12}  ->  {clock_reading(m)!r}")
    print()

# 3. The limit clock and the key function
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

LimitMoment = Tuple[int, Moment]  # <k, a> with a a moment of natClock(k)


def limit_key(x: LimitMoment) -> Ord:
    """key<k, a> = omega^k + reading(a)."""
    k, a = x
    return omega_pow_nat(k) + clock_reading(a)


def limit_lex_less(x: LimitMoment, y: LimitMoment) -> bool:
    """Lexicographic order on the dependent sum: compare depth first."""
    if x[0] != y[0]:
        return x[0] < y[0]
    return lex_less(x[1], y[1])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The monotone transfinite machine with closure ordinal omega^2
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cell = Tuple[int, int]  # cell (m, n) has arrival time omega*m + n


def arrival(cell: Cell) -> Ord:
    m, n = cell
    return (OMEGA * Ord.finite(m)) + Ord.finite(n)


def decode_cell(alpha: Ord) -> Cell:
    """The unique cell whose arrival time is alpha, for alpha < omega^2."""
    if not alpha < OMEGA_SQ:
        raise ValueError("only cells below omega^2 exist")
    m = 0
    for (e, c) in alpha.terms:
        if e == ONE:
            m = c
    return (m, alpha.finite_part)


def stage_contains(alpha: Ord, cell: Cell) -> bool:
    """Closed form of the stages: cell is on at time alpha iff arrival <= alpha."""
    return arrival(cell) <= alpha


def step(on: Iterable[Cell], universe: Sequence[Cell]) -> List[Cell]:
    """One transition: a cell switches on once all strictly earlier cells are on."""
    on_set = set(on)
    out: List[Cell] = []
    for c in universe:
        if all(d in on_set for d in universe if arrival(d) < arrival(c)):
            out.append(c)
    return out

@dataclass(frozen=True)

    def finite(n: int) -> "Ord":

    def power(exponent: "Ord", coeff: int = 1) -> "Ord":
        return Ord.zero() if coeff == 0 else Ord(((exponent, coeff),))

    def is_zero(self) -> bool:
        return not self.terms

        for (e1, c1), (e2, c2) in zip(self.terms, other.terms):
            k = e1.cmp(e2)
            if k:
                return k
            if c1 != c2:

        if len(self.terms) == len(other.terms):

        return -1 if len(self.terms) < len(other.terms) else 1

        return self.cmp(other) < 0

            return self
        lead = other.terms[0][0]
        kept = [(e, c) for (e, c) in self.terms if lead < e]
        tail = list(other.terms)
        same = [c for (e, c) in self.terms if e == lead]
        if same:

        return Ord(tuple(kept + tail))

        if self.is_zero:
            return "0"
        out: List[str] = []
        for (e, c) in self.terms:

            else:
                b = "w" if e == Ord.finite(1) else f"w^{e}"
                out.append(b if c == 1 else f"{b}*{c}")
        return " + ".join(out)

    for i, n in enumerate(moment):
        if n:
            out = out + Ord.power(Ord.finite(k - 1 - i), n)
    return out

    print("    bounds the order type, so the limit clock has value exactly omega^omega.\n")

def add(a: Ordinal, b: Ordinal) -> Ordinal:
    """Ordinal addition on base-omega numerals (left absorption below b's leading exponent)."""
    if not b:
        return dict(a)
    lead = max(b)
    out = {e: c for e, c in a.items() if e > lead}
    for e, c in b.items():
        out[e] = out.get(e, 0) + c

            return -1 if ca < cb else 1
    return 0


def rank(digits: Sequence[int]) -> Ordinal:
    k = len(digits)
    return {k - 1 - i: n for i, n in enumerate(digits) if n}

function ordAdd(a, b){

  const kept = a.filter(p => p[0] > lead);
  const same = a.filter(p => p[0] === lead);
  const tail = b.map(p => p.slice());

    if(a[i][1] !== b[i][1]) return a[i][1] < b[i][1] ? -1 : 1;

}
function readingOrd(ds){

document.getElementById('bigtick').onclick = () => {

document.getElementById('reset').onclick = () => { digits = new Array(K).fill(0); renderDigits(); };

/* ---------- section 2: hierarchy table ---------- */
function renderHier(){
  const rows = ['<tr><th>refinement depth</th><th>survival value</th><th>strictly above previous?</th></tr>'];
  for(let k = 0; k <= 6; k++){

let LK = 2, ldig = [0,0];
const ldEl = document.getElementById('ldigits');
function renderLimit(){
  document.getElementById('lklab').textContent = 'a moment of the depth-' + LK + ' clock';

function showKey(){

      "and the depths are cofinal, so the limit clock has length exactly \u03c9<sup>\u03c9</sup>.";

document.getElementById('lk').oninput = e => {
  LK = +e.target.value; ldig = new Array(Math.max(LK,1)).fill(0); renderLimit();
};

renderDigits(); renderHier(); renderStab(); renderLimit();
</script>

  "interactive_layout": "# How Long Can You Live? A Guided Tour of the Refinement Hierarchy

> **The setting.** You are Mortal. Before the game starts you hand your opponent, the Reaper, a
> *schedule*: a list of the moments of your life, laid out in order. Each round the Reaper
> advances one step down the list. You survive exactly as long as the list lasts.
>
> The only rule on the schedule is that it must be **well-ordered**: every non-empty collection
> of its moments has a first one. That is what makes the Reaper's march well defined. The
> **survival value** of a schedule is its *order type* — the ordinal it is a copy of — and
> Mortal can force survival to round $\alpha$ exactly when $\alpha \le \mathrm{val}(G)$.

Everything below is a consequence of that one setup. Let us build it up piece by piece.

---

## 1. Why counting fails and ordering works

Take the schedule $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$: one moment for each natural number. You survive round
$17$, round $10^{100}$, round $n$ for every finite $n$; there is no last moment. Its length is
the ordinal $\omega$.

Now take the schedule of *pairs* $(m, n)$ in dictionary order: infinitely many infinite runs,
one after another. It has exactly the same number of moments — you can match them up one for
one — but it is strictly longer as an ordering. Its length is $\omega^2$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why "the same size but strictly longer" is not a contradiction</b></summary>

Cardinality asks whether a bijection exists; order type asks whether an *order-preserving*
bijection exists. The pairs $(m,n)$ can be listed one by one — so they are countable — but any
such listing scrambles the order. Order type is a strictly finer invariant on well-orders than
cardinality, and it is the one that answers "who outlives whom". Background:
[ordinal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_number),
[order types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_type).
</details>

---

## 2. The refinement move

Here is the operation that generates the whole story. **Refine** a schedule by replacing each
of its moments with an entire copy of the natural-number clock: the new moments are pairs
$(x, n)$, ordered with the old coordinate dominant.

$$\mathrm{val}(\text{refinement of } G) \;=\; \omega \cdot \mathrm{val}(G).$$

Iterating $k$ times gives $\omega^k \cdot \mathrm{val}(G)$; applied to the natural-number
schedule, depth $k$ has value exactly $\omega^{k+1}$, and the hierarchy is **strict** — a
$j$-times refined Mortal cannot force survival to the round at which a $k$-times refined
Mortal dies, whenever $j < k$.

The widget below lets you feel this directly. Set a refinement depth, turn the odometer, and
watch its reading — the reading *is* the base-$\omega$ numeral of the moment you are standing
on. Then use the third panel to find the exact level at which refinement stops paying.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch: the refinement law and strictness</b></summary>

The lexicographic product $\mathrm{Lex}(A \times B)$ has order type
$\mathrm{type}(B)\cdot\mathrm{type}(A)$ — the *less* significant factor becomes the left factor
of the ordinal product. Refining by the natural-number clock therefore multiplies on the left
by $\omega$. Iterating, $\omega\cdot\omega^k = \omega^{1+k} = \omega^{k+1}$, where the last
step needs $1+k = k+1$, valid for finite $k$ only. Strictness is then strict monotonicity of
$\lambda \mapsto \omega^{\lambda}$ in the exponent, and the failure to force follows because
forcing survival to $\alpha$ is literally the inequality $\alpha \le \mathrm{val}(G)$.
</details>

---

## 3. What a bounded clock can measure

The $k$-times-refined single moment is just $\mathbb{N}^k$ in dictionary order — a base-$\omega$
odometer with $k$ digits. Its reading map

$$(n_1,\dots,n_k)\;\longmapsto\;\omega^{k-1}n_1 + \omega^{k-2}n_2 + \cdots + n_k$$

is an order isomorphism onto the ordinals below $\omega^k$. This gives the sharpest possible
statement about bounded clocks:

> **Clock Theorem.** A game can be timed by the $k$-digit odometer — its moments embed
> order-faithfully into $\mathbb{N}^k$ in dictionary order — **if and only if** its survival
> value is at most $\omega^k$. More generally, a game embeds into the ordinals below $o$ exactly
> when its value is at most $o$.

Forward, it is a hard ceiling; backward, the ceiling is attained. No slack in either direction.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 4. Climbing to $\omega^\omega$ — and the key that proves it

Play the depth-$0$ clock, then the depth-$1$ clock, then depth $2$, and so on: a moment is a
pair $\langle k, a\rangle$, ordered by depth first. Call this the **limit clock**.

> **Limit Theorem.** The limit clock has survival value exactly $\omega^\omega$, strictly above
> every finite depth.

The upper bound is delivered by one explicit formula, the **key**:

$$\mathrm{key}\langle k, a\rangle \;=\; \omega^k + \mathrm{rank}(a).$$

It does three jobs at once. It is strictly increasing (so the tangled order on this dependent
sum really is a well-order — no infinite descent hides in it); it lands strictly below
$\omega^\omega$, because $\mathrm{rank}(a) < \omega^k$ gives
$\mathrm{key} < \omega^k + \omega^k = \omega^k\cdot 2 \le \omega^{k+1} < \omega^\omega$; and it
is a finite symbolic computation you can actually run.

{{visualization:1}}

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The general mechanism: additively principal ordinals</b></summary>

This computation is an instance of a general theorem about stringing lives together. Track the
**landmarks** $\Lambda_0 = 0$, $\Lambda_{k+1} = \Lambda_k + \mathrm{val}(A_k)$ — the absolute
starting time of the $k$-th life. If $o$ is *additively principal* (no two ordinals below $o$
sum to $o$ or beyond; equivalently $o = \omega^a$), every $\mathrm{val}(A_k)$ is below $o$, and
the values are cofinal in $o$, then the concatenated life has value exactly $o$.

Additive principality is exactly the hypothesis that keeps the landmarks from escaping $o$;
cofinality is exactly what forces the value all the way up. Drop either and the theorem fails.
See [additively indecomposable ordinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additively_indecomposable_ordinal).
</details>

{{demo:1}}

---

## 5. The twist: refinement is not always a gain

Refinement looked like free money. It is not.

> **Fixed-Point Theorem.** Refining the limit clock buys Mortal nothing:
> $\omega\cdot\omega^\omega = \omega^\omega$. Hence it is **false** that refining by a clock of
> length greater than $1$ always strictly increases survival.

And there is an exact criterion for when the gain evaporates. Call $o$ *refinement stable* when
$\omega\cdot o = o$; within the pure scale, $\omega^a$ is stable **exactly when** $a$ is already
infinite. The reason is a single absorption identity: multiplying by $\omega$ replaces the
exponent $a$ by $1 + a$, and $1 + a = a$ holds precisely for infinite $a$.

That same identity explains all three headline results at once: the finite hierarchy is strict
because $1+k = k+1$; the limit is a fixed point because $1+\omega = \omega$; stability is
literally $1+a = a$.

Absorption also makes concatenation non-commutative: a moment tacked on *after* an endless life
is a genuine gain, $\omega + 1 > \omega$, while the same moment placed *before* it is invisible,
$1 + \omega = \omega$. When you get the extra moment matters more than getting it.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 6. The same ordinals, now running as a machine

Give every moment of the $\omega^2$-clock a cell. Run a machine that at successor times applies
one rule and at limit times unions everything that came before. The rule: **a cell switches on
once all strictly earlier cells are on.**

The natural question is the **closure ordinal**: the first time after which nothing new ever
happens. Play with it below — step through finite times, jump past $\omega$, and try to make it
stall early. You cannot.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **Closure Theorem.** A cell is on at time $\alpha$ exactly when its arrival time (its position
> in the clock) is at most $\alpha$. Hence no stage before $\omega^2$ is terminal, stage
> $\omega^2$ is, and the closure ordinal is *exactly* $\omega^2$. Moreover the machine is
> faithful: its well-order of reachable times is order-isomorphic to the schedule of the game it
> realises, so the closure ordinal equals that game's survival value.

{{visualization:0}}

{{algorithm:3}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why exactness is the interesting half</b></summary>

An upper bound alone would leave open that the system stalls earlier. The lower half — no stage
below $\omega^2$ is terminal — uses that $\omega^2$ is additively principal: if
$\alpha < \omega^2$ then $\alpha + 1 < \omega^2$, so *some* cell has arrival time exactly
$\alpha+1$. That cell is off at $\alpha$ and on at $\alpha+1$: an explicit witness that the
configuration changed. Related reading:
[infinite-time computation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite-time_Turing_machine),
[closure ordinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_number).
</details>

---

## 7. Nothing is lost in passing to the ordinal

One might worry that "survival value" throws information away. It does not.

> **Completeness.** Every schedule is order-isomorphic to the canonical clock of its own value.
> Hence two games have equal value if and only if their schedules are order-isomorphic — and
> every ordinal is the value of some game.

So the theory of survival games *is* the theory of ordinals, faithfully and surjectively. Every
statement about who outlives whom is a statement of ordinal arithmetic, and conversely.

---

## 8. Run it all yourself

The demonstration below reproduces every result on this page with exact ordinal arithmetic:
the refinement law, the strict hierarchy, the odometer readings, the key bound, the fixed point,
the non-commutativity of concatenation, the machine's stages, and the landmark bookkeeping of
the general limit theorem.

{{demo:0}}

---

## Where this goes next

* **A transfinite tower.** Index refinement by ordinals rather than natural numbers, refining by
  $\omega$ at successors and taking the dependent lexicographic sum at limits. The key
  $\omega^\delta + \mathrm{rank}(a)$ is definable uniformly in the level, so the conjecture is
  that level $\delta$ has value $\omega^{\delta+1}$ and the tower's own limit is exactly
  $\varepsilon_0$ — the first ordinal with $\omega^\varepsilon = \varepsilon$.
* **Stability in general.** The criterion should read off the Cantor normal form: $\omega\cdot o
  = o$ exactly when every exponent of $o$ is infinite. Stability is a *tail* condition, not a
  size condition.
* **Cheaper machines.** The machine above may consult its whole earlier configuration.
  Restricting to steps presented by a fixed finite amount of local data should make some
  ordinals unreachable as closure ordinals — a genuine clockability gap.

**The moral.** Buying time by making finer distinctions works, brilliantly, one level at a time.
It stops working the instant your distinctions are already infinitely fine. After that the only
way up is to concatenate something genuinely new.

# Persistent Homology of the Prime Point Cloud

The prime numbers `2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …` form a point cloud on the real line, the
`n`-th prime sitting at position `p_n`.  Sweeping a scale parameter `ε ≥ 0` and
joining two points whenever they lie within distance `ε` produces the
Vietoris–Rips filtration of the cloud.  Its degree-zero persistent homology
records how the connected components merge as `ε` grows: a *bar* is born when a
component appears and dies when it is absorbed by an older one.

For a point cloud on a line the entire zero-dimensional barcode is governed by
the *gaps* between consecutive points.  This file makes that statement precise
and specialises it to the primes.

## Main results

* `PrimePH.line_component_iff` — **single-linkage on a line**: two indices `i ≤ j`
  lie in the same `ε`-component if and only if every consecutive gap between them
  is at most `ε`.  This is the combinatorial heart of the barcode: components are
  exactly the maximal runs of small gaps.

* `PrimePH.adjacent_component_iff` — the death scale of the merge between the
  components of neighbouring points `i` and `i+1` is exactly the gap
  `p_{i+1} - p_i`.  Thus the finite `H_0` bar lengths are precisely the gaps.

* `PrimePH.death_scale_eq_primeGap` — for the prime cloud the death scale of the
  `i`-th adjacent merge equals the `i`-th prime gap `p_{i+1} - p_i`, linking the
  topology to the arithmetic gap sequence of `BoundedGaps.lean`.

* `PrimePH.twinPrime_iff_infinitely_many_gap_two` — the **twin prime conjecture**
  is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many prime gaps equal to `2`; via
  `death_scale_eq_primeGap` these are exactly the `H_0` bars whose death scale is
  `2`.  So the twin prime conjecture is the statement that the prime barcode has
  infinitely many bars of length `2`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis.  The zero-dimensional persistent homology of a point cloud on ℝ is
determined by the gap sequence; for the primes the twin prime conjecture should
translate into a statement about the barcode.

Experiment.  We formalised the Vietoris–Rips adjacency `|p a - p b| ≤ ε` and its
connectivity closure, and proved the single-linkage characterisation via a
covering argument on integer intervals: an edge `a — b` certifies every gap
strictly between `a` and `b`, and the interval `[min a b, max a b)` is always
covered by the two sub-intervals produced along a transitive step.

Analysis.  The line makes the barcode collapse to the gap multiset because gaps
are positive and telescope: `p_{k+1} − p_k ≤ p_b − p_a` whenever `a ≤ k < b`.
The twin prime bridge reduces to the arithmetic fact that consecutive primes are
`2` apart exactly at a twin pair, using `next_prime_le_of_prime_lt` from the
catalog to identify the successor prime.

Critique.  The connectivity relation is the genuine reflexive–transitive–
symmetric closure of the Rips graph, not a definitional restatement of the gap
condition, so the equivalence is a theorem rather than a `rfl`.  The twin prime
equivalence is stated over the honest sets and proved in both directions.

Synthesis.  "Primes have topology": their gap sequence *is* the `H_0` barcode,
and the twin prime conjecture is the assertion that the length-`2` bar recurs
forever.

import Mathlib
import Novelty.NumberTheory.BoundedGaps

open Relation

namespace PrimePH

/-- Vietoris–Rips adjacency at scale `ε`: two indices are joined when the
corresponding points lie within distance `ε`. -/
def RipsAdj (p : ℕ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ) (a b : ℕ) : Prop := |p a - p b| ≤ ε

/-- Being in the same `ε`-connected component: the reflexive–transitive closure
of the (symmetric) Rips adjacency relation. -/
def RipsConn (p : ℕ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ) : ℕ → ℕ → Prop :=
  Relation.ReflTransGen (RipsAdj p ε)

/-
A single gap is dominated by any endpoint difference straddling it.
-/
lemma gap_le_sub {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {a b k : ℕ}
    (h1 : a ≤ k) (h2 : k < b) : p (k + 1) - p k ≤ p b - p a := by
  linarith [ hp.monotone h1, hp.monotone ( Nat.succ_le_of_lt h2 ) ]

/-
An `ε`-edge `a — b` certifies that every consecutive gap strictly between
`a` and `b` is at most `ε`.
-/
lemma edge_gaps {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ} {a b : ℕ}
    (h : RipsAdj p ε a b) :
    ∀ k, min a b ≤ k → k < max a b → p (k + 1) - p k ≤ ε := by
  cases le_total a b <;> simp_all +decide [ RipsAdj ];
  · intro k hk₁ hk₂; linarith [ hp.monotone ( show k + 1 ≤ b by linarith ), hp.monotone ( show a ≤ k by linarith ), abs_le.mp h ] ;
  · intro k hk₁ hk₂; linarith [ abs_le.mp h, hp.monotone hk₁, hp.monotone ( Nat.le_succ k ), hp.monotone hk₂ ] ;

/-
Backward direction of single-linkage: small gaps chain into connectivity.
-/
lemma chain_of_gaps {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 ≤ ε)
    (i n : ℕ) (h : ∀ k, i ≤ k → k < i + n → p (k + 1) - p k ≤ ε) :
    RipsConn p ε i (i + n) := by
  induction' n with n ih generalizing i;
  · exact Relation.ReflTransGen.refl;
  · convert Relation.ReflTransGen.tail ( ih i fun k hk₁ hk₂ => h k hk₁ ( by linarith ) ) _ using 1;
    exact abs_sub_le_iff.mpr ⟨ by linarith! [ h ( i + n ) ( by linarith ) ( by linarith ), hp ( Nat.lt_succ_self ( i + n ) ) ], by linarith! [ h ( i + n ) ( by linarith ) ( by linarith ), hp ( Nat.lt_succ_self ( i + n ) ) ] ⟩

/-
Forward direction of single-linkage: connectivity forces all intermediate
gaps to be small.
-/
lemma gaps_of_chain {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ} {a b : ℕ}
    (h : RipsConn p ε a b) :
    ∀ k, min a b ≤ k → k < max a b → p (k + 1) - p k ≤ ε := by
  have := @edge_gaps;
  induction h <;> simp_all +decide;
  grind

/-
**Single-linkage clustering on a line.**  For a strictly increasing point
cloud, indices `i ≤ j` lie in the same `ε`-component precisely when every
consecutive gap between them is at most `ε`.
-/
theorem line_component_iff {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 ≤ ε)
    {i j : ℕ} (hij : i ≤ j) :
    RipsConn p ε i j ↔ ∀ k, i ≤ k → k < j → p (k + 1) - p k ≤ ε := by
  constructor;
  · exact fun h k hk₁ hk₂ => gaps_of_chain hp h k ( by aesop ) ( by aesop );
  · exact fun h => by simpa only [ Nat.add_sub_cancel' hij ] using chain_of_gaps hp hε i ( j - i ) fun k hk₁ hk₂ => h k hk₁ ( by omega ) ;

/-
The merge of neighbouring points `i` and `i+1` happens at scale `ε` exactly
when `ε` reaches the gap `p_{i+1} - p_i`; i.e. the `i`-th finite `H_0` bar has
death scale equal to that gap.
-/
theorem adjacent_component_iff {p : ℕ → ℝ} (hp : StrictMono p) {ε : ℝ}
    (hε : 0 ≤ ε) (i : ℕ) :
    RipsConn p ε i (i + 1) ↔ p (i + 1) - p i ≤ ε := by
  convert line_component_iff hp hε ( Nat.le_succ i ) using 1;
  exact ⟨ fun h k hk₁ hk₂ => by rw [ show k = i by linarith ] ; exact h, fun h => h i le_rfl ( Nat.lt_succ_self i ) ⟩

/-! ### The prime point cloud -/

/-- The prime point cloud: the `n`-th prime placed on the real line. -/
noncomputable def P (n : ℕ) : ℝ := (Nat.nth Nat.Prime n : ℝ)

/-
The prime positions are strictly increasing.
-/
lemma P_strictMono : StrictMono P := by
  exact fun a b hab => Nat.cast_lt.mpr ( Nat.nth_strictMono ( Nat.infinite_setOf_prime ) hab )

/-
The death scale of the `i`-th adjacent merge in the prime barcode equals the
`i`-th prime gap of `BoundedGaps.lean`.
-/
theorem death_scale_eq_primeGap (i : ℕ) :
    P (i + 1) - P i = (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) := by
  unfold P TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap;
  rw [ Nat.cast_sub ( Nat.nth_monotone ( Nat.infinite_setOf_prime ) ( Nat.le_succ _ ) ) ]

/-
Neighbouring primes merge at scale `ε` iff `ε` is at least their gap.
-/
theorem prime_adjacent_component_iff {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 ≤ ε) (i : ℕ) :
    RipsConn P ε i (i + 1) ↔ (TwinPrimeGaps.primeGap i : ℝ) ≤ ε := by
  grind +suggestions

/-! ### The twin prime bar -/

/-
**The twin prime conjecture as a barcode statement.**  There are infinitely
many twin prime pairs `(p, p+2)` if and only if there are infinitely many indices
`n` with prime gap exactly `2` — equivalently, infinitely many `H_0` bars of
death scale `2`.

/-!
# Translations between proof systems, tight pigeonhole codes, and large antichains

This file continues the resource-bounded reading of "mind tools" begun in
`Catalog/Novelty/MindToolsBoundedApprehension.lean`, which in turn builds on the
extensional framework of `Catalog/Logic/MindTools.lean`.

Three further items of the stated programme are carried out.

* **Interpretations between theories (extension 4).**  A `Translation` between
  proof systems is a conclusion-preserving map of proofs together with a
  monotone bound on the size blow-up.  Translations transport theories
  (`Translation.theory_subset`) and, crucially, transport *bounded apprehension*
  with a computable budget change (`Translation.apprehends_subset`).  This
  separates "expressive convenience" from genuine cognitive extension: a budget
  gap that survives every monotone bound is exactly an obstruction to
  translation (`not_translation_of_apprehension_gap`).

* **Tightness of the counting certificate (extension 3).**  The pigeonhole
  certificate of the previous file guarantees an inaccessible sentence below
  `2 ^ (b + 1)`.  Here the bound is shown to be *exactly attained*: the binary
  numeral code `bcode` apprehends, at budget `b`, precisely the numbers
  `< 2 ^ (b + 1) - 1`, so its least inaccessible sentence is `2 ^ (b + 1) - 1`
  (`bcode_isLeast_not_apprehended`).

* **Antichains of every size (extension 7, quantitative).**  For any index type
  the singleton theories are pairwise incomparable while being ordinal-ranked,
  hence well-founded: well-foundedness of a hierarchy of tools never implies
  comparability, no matter how many tools are present
  (`exists_ordinalRanked_antichain`).
-/

namespace MindTools
namespace Bounded

universe u

variable {Sentence : Type u}

/-! ## Translations (interpretations) between proof systems -/

/-- A **translation** of proof systems: a map on derivations preserving
conclusions, whose size blow-up is controlled by a monotone bound.  This is the
resource-sensitive analogue of an interpretation of theories. -/
structure Translation (P Q : ProofSystem Sentence) where
  /-- The map on derivations. -/
  map : P.Proof → Q.Proof
  /-- Translation preserves what is proved. -/
  conclusion_map : ∀ p, Q.conclusion (map p) = P.conclusion p
  /-- The size blow-up bound. -/
  bound : ℕ → ℕ
  /-- The bound is monotone. -/
  bound_mono : Monotone bound
  /-- The blow-up really is bounded. -/
  size_map_le : ∀ p, Q.size (map p) ≤ bound (P.size p)

namespace Translation

variable {P Q R : ProofSystem Sentence}

/-- The identity translation, with no blow-up. -/
def id (P : ProofSystem Sentence) : Translation P P where
  map := _root_.id
  conclusion_map _ := rfl
  bound := _root_.id
  bound_mono := monotone_id
  size_map_le _ := le_rfl

/-- Translations compose, the bounds composing as well. -/
def comp (t : Translation P Q) (u : Translation Q R) : Translation P R where
  map := u.map ∘ t.map
  conclusion_map p := by
    simp [u.conclusion_map, t.conclusion_map]
  bound := u.bound ∘ t.bound
  bound_mono := u.bound_mono.comp t.bound_mono
  size_map_le p :=
    (u.size_map_le (t.map p)).trans (u.bound_mono (t.size_map_le p))

/-- A translation makes the target theory contain the source theory: this is the
extensional shadow of an interpretation. -/
theorem theory_subset (t : Translation P Q) :
    (theory P).provable ⊆ (theory Q).provable := by
  rintro s ⟨p, rfl⟩
  exact ⟨t.map p, t.conclusion_map p⟩

/-- The essential resource-sensitive statement: apprehension at budget `b` in
the source is apprehension at budget `bound b` in the target. -/
theorem apprehends_subset (t : Translation P Q) (b : ℕ) :
    (apprehends P b).direct ⊆ (apprehends Q (t.bound b)).direct := by
  rintro s ⟨p, hp, rfl⟩
  exact ⟨t.map p, (t.size_map_le p).trans (t.bound_mono hp), t.conclusion_map p⟩

/-- Consequently a translation with bound `f` collapses every apprehension gap
of shape `(b, f b)`. -/
theorem not_apprehension_gap (t : Translation P Q) {b : ℕ} {s : Sentence}
    (hs : s ∈ (apprehends P b).direct) : s ∈ (apprehends Q (t.bound b)).direct :=
  t.apprehends_subset b hs

end Translation

/-- **Certificate for non-translatability.**  If some sentence is apprehended in
`P` within budget `b` but is not apprehended in `Q` within budget `f b`, then no
translation of `P` into `Q` has size bound `f`.  A surviving budget gap is thus
exactly an obstruction to bounded interpretation — the precise sense in which a
cognitive separation is more than expressive convenience. -/
theorem not_translation_of_apprehension_gap {P Q : ProofSystem Sentence}
    (f : ℕ → ℕ) {b : ℕ} {s : Sentence}
    (hs : s ∈ (apprehends P b).direct) (hgap : s ∉ (apprehends Q (f b)).direct) :
    ¬ ∃ t : Translation P Q, t.bound = f := by
  rintro ⟨t, rfl⟩
  exact hgap (t.apprehends_subset b hs)

theorem isMindTool_of_translation {P Q : ProofSystem Sentence}
    (t : Translation P Q) (b : ℕ) {s : Sentence}
    (hs : s ∈ (theory Q).provable) (hs' : s ∉ (apprehends Q (t.bound b)).direct) :
    IsMindTool (theory Q) (apprehends P b) := by
